name: ragel
why: A state machine compiler that turns regex-like descriptions into fast parsers, a deep and old-school tool for seeing how parsers work.

brief.what_it_is: Ragel is a state machine compiler. You write a machine description that mixes regular-expression operators (union, concatenation, Kleene star) with embedded actions, which are small blocks of host-language code attached to points in the machine. Ragel takes that description and emits C, C++, or x86_64 GNU assembly that runs the machine with no runtime dependencies. The page's example takes a number grammar with actions as input and outputs a chain of goto-based states, and it can also visualize the machine with Graphviz.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage positions Ragel for writing robust protocol implementations, parsing data formats, lexical analysis of programming languages, and validating user input. Its stated goal is to let developers describe recognizers declaratively and run code at exact points during recognition.
brief.how_it_works: Ragel compiles the regular expressions to a deterministic finite automaton and associates the embedded actions with the transitions of that automaton. The generated code can be table-driven or control-flow-driven, and the machine can be minimized with Hopcroft's algorithm. The page also notes operators for controlling non-determinism, building scanners, and statechart-style machines, plus jumping or calling into other parts of a machine from inside an action.

brief.install_notes: Ragel 7.1.0 ships inside the Colm Suite, a calendar-versioned bundle, so building it means running autogen.sh, configure, make, and make install. Use --disable-install-colm if you only want ragel. CMake 3.16 or later is an alternative to the autotools path, with options listed in the README. The stable Ragel 6.11 tarball is also offered separately. No accounts, hardware, or runtimes are mentioned beyond the build toolchain.
brief.standout: Ragel embeds actions at arbitrary points in a regular language without breaking its syntax, and the generated code has no dependencies and no license requirement on its output. Its visualization and statechart support set it apart from simpler regex engines.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists a stable Ragel 6.11 release dated July 2026 and a development Ragel 7.1.0 release dated August 2026, with a link to a GitHub discussions forum for questions. I did not check the repository commit history.
brief.caveats: Generated assembly targets only GNU, x86_64, System V ABI. Building the full Colm Suite is needed to get Ragel 7, and the page does not give its dependency list. Ragel 6 remains under GPL v2 while Ragel 7 uses MIT, so licensing depends on the version chosen. The original mailing list is no longer running, so questions go to GitHub discussions or the archive.
quotes: Ragel compiles executable finite state machines from regular languages.
Ragel provides a very flexible interface to the host language that attempts to place minimal restrictions on how the generated code is integrated into the application.
Use of Ragel makes absolutely no requirement about the license of generated code.

judge.reason: Ragel turns regular-language descriptions with embedded actions into visualizable, dependency-free state-machine code, making a compelling hands-on way to explore parser construction.

entry.title: Ragel
entry.tldr: Ragel compiles regex-like machine descriptions with embedded code actions into dependency-free C, C++ or assembly state machines, a hands-on way to see how parsers work.
entry.deeper_look:
Ragel is a state machine compiler. You write a machine description that mixes regular-expression operators (union, concatenation, Kleene star) with embedded actions, which are small blocks of host-language code attached to points in the machine. Ragel turns that into C, C++, or x86_64 GNU assembly that runs the machine with no runtime dependencies. It can also draw the machine with Graphviz.

The idea underneath is that a regular expression is a deterministic finite automaton in disguise. Ragel compiles your expressions to a DFA and attaches your actions to its transitions, so your code runs at exact points during recognition rather than after a match is complete. The generated code can be table-driven or built from gotos, and the machine can be minimized with Hopcroft's algorithm.

The homepage positions it for protocol implementations, data format parsing, lexical analysis of programming languages, and input validation. It also has operators for controlling non-determinism, building scanners, and statechart-style machines, plus jumping or calling into other parts of a machine from inside an action.

In the project's words: "Ragel compiles executable finite state machines from regular languages." Reading the goto-based output for a small number grammar is a direct look at what a parser actually is once the notation is gone.
entry.install:
brew install ragel
# Homebrew installs a packaged release. The upstream project builds Ragel 7 from the Colm Suite with autogen.sh, configure, make, and make install. No accounts or hardware needed beyond a build toolchain.
